newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil gov't wants votes, despite re-election heat.
newsitem.headline: Brazil gov't wants votes, despite re-election heat.

text.p: The Brazilian government hopes to get two controversial bills through the lower house this week although maneuvering by opponents of re-election is likely to hog the headlines, an aide to a senior congressional whip said.
One of the bills creates the Temporary Labor Contract which does away with several employer contributions for staff hired for a maximum of six months.
The government says the bill will help reduce unemployment in Brazil while unions argue it strips workers of their rights.
The other bill sets down the small print of a constitutional amendment approved last year that opened up Brazil's inland shipping sector to foreign companies.
Both bills have been bogged down by opposition within Congress and the labor movement but are likely to be voted by the Chamber of Deputies on Wednesday, the spokeswoman for Deputy Benito Gama said.

The spokeswoman said the government was anxious to show that re-election was not its only concern and other bills should be approved by the end of the year. "From now until December the government will keep up a fast pace in Congress," she said.

One important bill due to be sent to Congress shortly would detail Brazil's plans to privatize its telecommunications industry. A Communications Ministry official said the bill might be sent to Congress this week.
Government leaders were due to discuss Tuesday how to get an agreement among allied parties for lower house approval of a civil service reform.
The reform would allow state and municipal governments to fire currently unsackable employees and cut their payroll spending.

But many deputies, who enjoy special pension privileges they accumulated during public service careers, balk at a proposed 10,800-reais ceiling on monthly pay and pensions which would reduce their earnings.
The star of the week was likely to prove Paulo Maluf, the outgoing mayor of Sao Paulo who hopes to defeat the amendment allowing re-election and win the 1998 presidential race himself.
Maluf was due to address Tuesday a lower house committee which is mulling a draft version of the re-election amendment.
